Zedekiah Consults Jeremiah What Is to Be the Event of the War: God's Answer.</title> <div sID="gen17888" type="x-p"/> Written probably when, after having repulsed the Egyptians who brought succors to the Jews (<reference osisRef="Jer.37.5-Jer.37.8">Jr 37:5-8</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.7">2Ki 24:7</reference>), the Chaldees were a second time advancing against Jerusalem, but were not yet closely besieging it (<reference osisRef="Jer.21.4">Jr 21:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.21.13">13</reference>) [Rosenmuller]. This chapter probably ought to be placed between the thirty-seventh and thirty-eight chapters; since what the "princes," in <reference osisRef="Jer.38.2">Jr 38:2</reference>, represent Jeremiah as having said, is exactly what we find in <reference osisRef="Jer.21.9">Jr 21:9</reference>. Moreover, the same persons as here (<reference osisRef="Jer.21.1">Jr 21:1</reference>) are mentioned in <reference osisRef="Jer.37.3">Jr 37:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.38.1">38:1</reference>, namely, Pashur and Zephaniah. What is here more fully related is there simply referred to in the historical narrative. Compare <reference osisRef="Jer.52.24">Jr 52:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.18">2Ki 25:18</reference> [Maurer].<div eID="gen17888" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17889" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10040"/><hi type="bold">1. Zedekiah--</hi>a prince having some reverence for sacred things, for which reason he sends an honorable embassy to Jeremiah; but not having moral courage to obey his better impulses.<div eID="gen17889" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17890" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Pashur--</hi>son of Melchiah, of the fifth order of priests, distinct from Pashur, son of Immer (<reference osisRef="Jer.20.1">Jr 20:1</reference>), of the sixteenth order (<reference osisRef="1Chr.24.9">1Ch 24:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.24.14">14</reference>).<div eID="gen17890" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17891" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Zephaniah--</hi>of the twenty-fourth order. They are designated, not by their father, but by their family (<reference osisRef="1Chr.24.18">1Ch 24:18</reference>). <div eID="gen17891" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: CHAPTER 21 Jr 21:1-44. Zedekiah Consults Jeremiah What Is to Be the Event of the War: God's Answer. Written probably when, after having repulsed the Egyptians who brought succors to the Jews ( Jr 37:5-8 ; 2Ki 24:7 ), the Chaldees were a second time advancing against Jerusalem, but were not yet closely besieging it ( Jr 21:4 , 13 ) [Rosenmuller]. This chapter probably ought to be placed between the thirty-seventh and thirty-eight chapters; since what the "princes," in Jr 38:2 , represent Jeremiah as having said, is exactly what we find in Jr 21:9 . Moreover, the same persons as here ( Jr 21:1 ) are mentioned in Jr 37:3 ; 38:1 , namely, Pashur and Zephaniah. What is here more fully related is there simply referred to in the historical narrative. Compare Jr 52:24 ; 2Ki 25:18 [Maurer]. 1. Zedekiah-- a prince having some reverence for sacred things, for which reason he sends an honorable embassy to Jeremiah; but not having moral courage to obey his better impulses. Pashur-- son of Melchiah, of the fifth order of priests, distinct from Pashur, son of Immer ( Jr 20:1 ), of the sixteenth order ( 1Ch 24:9 , 14 ). Zephaniah-- of the twenty-fourth order. They are designated, not by their father, but by their family ( 1Ch 24:18 ).

Nebuchadrezzar--</hi>the more usual way of spelling the name in Jeremiah than Nebuchadnezzar. From Persiac roots, meaning either "Nebo, the chief of the gods," or, "Nebo, the god of fire." He was son of Nabopolassar, who committed the command of the army against Egypt, at Carchemish, and against Judea, to the crown prince.<div eID="gen17892" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17893" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">according to all his wondrous works--</hi>Zedekiah hopes for God's special interposition, such as was vouchsafed to Hezekiah against Sennacherib (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.35">2Ki 19:35</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.36">36</reference>).<div eID="gen17893" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17894" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he--</hi>Nebuchadnezzar.<div eID="gen17894" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17895" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">go up from us--</hi>rise up from the siege which he sat down to lay (<reference osisRef="Jer.37.5">Jr 37:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.37.11">11</reference>, Margin; <reference osisRef="Num.16.24">Nu 16:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.16.27">27</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.19">1Ki 15:19</reference>, Margin). <div eID="gen17895" type="x-p"/>

He was son of Nabopolassar, who committed the command of the army against Egypt, at Carchemish, and against Judea, to the crown prince. according to all his wondrous works-- Zedekiah hopes for God's special interposition, such as was vouchsafed to Hezekiah against Sennacherib ( 2Ki 19:35 , 36 ). he-- Nebuchadnezzar. go up from us-- rise up from the siege which he sat down to lay ( Jr 37:5 , 11 , Margin; Nu 16:24 , 27 ; 1Ki 15:19 , Margin).

God of Israel--</hi>Those "wondrous works" (<reference osisRef="Jer.21.2">Jr 21:2</reference>) do not belong to you; God is faithful; it is you who forfeit the privileges of the covenant by unfaithfulness. "God will always remain the God of Israel, though He destroy thee and thy people" [Calvin].<div eID="gen17896" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17897" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">turn back the weapons--</hi>I will turn them to a very different use from what you intend them. With them you now fight against the Chaldees "without the walls" (the Jewish defenders being as yet able to sally forth more freely, and defend the fountains outside the walls in the valley under Mount Zion; see <reference osisRef="Jer.21.13">Jr 21:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.19.6">Jr 19:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.19.7">7</reference>); but soon ye shall be driven back within the city [Maurer], and "in the midst" of it, I will cause all your arms to be gathered in one place ("I will assemble them," namely, your arms) by the Chaldean conquerors [Grotius], who shall slay you with those very arms [Menochius]. <div eID="gen17897" type="x-p"/>

The Jews shall have not merely the Chaldees, but Jehovah Himself in wrath at their provocations, fighting against them. entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10045"/><div sID="gen17902" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10045"/>8. "Life," if ye surrender; "death," if ye persist in opposing the Chaldees (compare <reference osisRef="Deut.30.19">De 30:19</reference>). The individuality of Jeremiah's mission from God is shown in that he urges to unconditional surrender; whereas all former prophets had urged the people to oppose their invaders (<reference osisRef="Isa.7.16">Is 7:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.37.33">37:33</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.37.35">35</reference>). <div eID="gen17902" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10048"/><div sID="gen17907" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10048"/><hi type="bold">12. house of David--</hi>the royal family and all in office about the king. He calls them so, because it was the greater disgrace that they had so degenerated from the piety of their forefather, David; and to repress their glorying in their descent from him, as if they were therefore inviolable; but God will not spare them as apostates.<div eID="gen17907" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17908" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the morning--</hi>alluding to the time of dispensing justice (<reference osisRef="Job.24.17">Job 24:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.101.8">Psa 101:8</reference>); but the sense is mainly proverbial, for "with promptness" (<reference osisRef="Ps.90.14">Psa 90:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.143.8">143:8</reference>). Maurer translates, "every morning."<div eID="gen17908" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17909" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lest my fury ... like fire--</hi>Already it was kindled, and the decree of God gone forth against the city (<reference osisRef="Jer.21.4">Jr 21:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.21.5">5</reference>), but the king and his house may yet be preserved by repentance and reformation. God urges to righteousness, not as if they can thereby escape punishment wholly, but as the condition of a mitigation of it. <div eID="gen17909" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10049"/><div sID="gen17910" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10049"/><hi type="bold">13. inhabitant of the valley, and rock of the plain--</hi>Jerusalem personified; situated for the most part on hills, with valleys at the bottom of them, as the valley of Hinnom, &c.; and beyond the valleys and mountains again, a position most fortified by nature, whence the inhabitants fancied themselves beyond the reach of enemies; but since God is "against" them, their position will avail nothing for them. The "valley" between Mount Zion and Moriah is called Tyropoeon. Robinson takes, "rock of the plain" as Mount Zion, on which is a level tract of some extent. It is appropriately here referred to, being the site of the royal residence of the "house of David," addressed (<reference osisRef="Jer.21.12">Jr 21:12</reference>). <div eID="gen17910" type="x-p"/>
